result: Participants' timing estimates systematically regressed towards the mean of the tested intervals, with shorter durations overestimated and longer durations underestimated. This regression effect was observed in all participants and is consistent with prior literature on timing behavior.
evaluation: Claims C17, C36, C37, and C127 collectively demonstrate the behavioral regression effect with statistical support (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). The findings are well-documented with appropriate statistical tests (one-sample t-tests) and are consistent with cited prior work (Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2010).

result: Task performance improved over time at the group level, with both accuracy and precision increasing. Behavioral responses became more optimal, balancing specificity and regularization objectives as participants progressed through the experiment.
evaluation: Claims C45, C122, and C123 are supported by statistical analyses using linear mixed-effects models showing significant improvements in accuracy (F(1)=15.127, p=1.3×10⁻⁴) and precision (F(1)=20.189, p=6.1×10⁻⁵) over time, with appropriate effect sizes reported (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).

result: Anterior hippocampal activity was modulated by behavioral feedback received in each trial, with higher-accuracy feedback resulting in stronger activity. This effect was observed in both ROI and whole-brain voxel-wise analyses.
evaluation: Claims C2, C18, C51, and C96 are supported by convergent evidence from independent ROI analyses (anterior HPC: t(33)=-3.80, p=5.9×10⁻⁴, d=-0.65) and whole-brain voxel-wise analyses (Figure 2A, 2B). The results were robust across multiple model specifications (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).

result: Hippocampal functional connectivity with motor cortex, parahippocampal gyrus, medial parietal lobe, and cerebellum was modulated by feedback, with stronger co-fluctuations during poor performance. Notably, functional connectivity scaled negatively with feedback valence while absolute activity scaled positively.
evaluation: Claims C19, C55-58, C103-106, and C109 are supported by PPI analyses showing task-dependent functional connectivity patterns (Figure 2C). The dissociation between absolute activity and connectivity measures is well-documented and suggests distinct but related processes, though the mechanistic interpretation remains speculative.

result: Hippocampal activity reflected performance improvements across trials and demonstrated a direct link between hippocampal processing, feedback received, and behavioral improvements over time.
evaluation: Claims C3, C20, C77, and C100 are supported by analyses showing hippocampal activity tracked behavioral improvements (Figure 3). The statistical evidence includes both whole-brain and ROI analyses with appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons.

result: Posterior hippocampal activity signaled performance improvements independent of the specific TTC interval tested, reflecting TTC-independent updating processes that support regularization rather than interval-specific learning.
evaluation: Claims C4, C21, C119, and C137 are supported by parametric regressor analyses showing TTC-independent updating signals in posterior hippocampus (t(33)=2.81, p=0.004, d=0.48) but not anterior hippocampus (Figure 3B). The distinction between TTC-specific and TTC-independent processes is well-demonstrated.

result: Anterior hippocampal activity reflected the magnitude of the behavioral regression effect on a trial-by-trial basis, with stronger activity when TTC estimates were more biased towards the mean of sampled intervals.
evaluation: Claims C5, C22, C64, C125, and C130 are supported by parametric analyses showing anterior hippocampal activity tracked the regression effect (t(33)=-5.55, p=3.6×10⁻⁶, d=-0.95) (Figure 4). The negative beta estimates correctly indicate stronger activity with greater bias towards the mean.

result: Striatal subregions showed distinct patterns of TTC-specific versus TTC-independent updating, with caudate signaling interval-specific improvements and putamen showing both processes. Striatal regions tracked response accuracy but not regression-to-mean biases.
evaluation: Claims C23, C24, C53, C60, C119, C120, C131, and C134 are supported by whole-brain and ROI analyses showing differential striatal involvement (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 4A). Statistical tests with appropriate corrections demonstrate significant effects in caudate (TTC-specific: t(33)=5.95, p=5.6×10⁻⁷) and putamen (both processes).

result: Hippocampal activity co-fluctuated with putamen and thalamus specifically during behavioral improvements, suggesting feedback-dependent changes in functional connectivity with task-relevant regions.
evaluation: Claims C61 and C107 are supported by PPI analyses showing TTC-independent connectivity between hippocampus and subcortical regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). Statistical tests show significant effects in putamen (t(33)=2.79, p=0.004) and thalamus (t(33)=2.71, p=0.005) with appropriate corrections.

result: The feedback distribution was balanced across TTC levels and over-/underestimation trials, with no systematic autocorrelation between successive trials, confirming the experimental design controlled for potential confounds.
evaluation: Claims C48, C49, and C50 are supported by control analyses showing balanced feedback distributions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, 1C) and no significant n-1 autocorrelation (t(33)=1.03, p=0.312). These methodological controls strengthen the interpretation of the main findings.

result: Eye-tracking control analyses confirmed that fixation quality did not differ systematically across speed levels or accuracy levels, and fixation error did not correlate with the regression effect or task performance.
evaluation: Claim C70 is supported by comprehensive eye-tracking analyses using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Spearman correlations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). All comparisons were non-significant after FWE correction, ruling out viewing behavior as a confound.

result: The study employed a well-designed TTC estimation task with 34 participants (after exclusions), using four speed levels, scaled feedback, and 768 trials per participant. The sample size was justified by prior work and the study received appropriate ethical approval.
evaluation: Claims C25-34 and C142-146 describe methodological details that are clearly documented and appropriate. The task design incorporated Weber-Fechner scaling for feedback (C31, C32), ensuring balanced feedback distributions across intervals. Sample size justification via prior work (C144) is reasonable for fMRI studies.

result: The hippocampus supports rapid encoding of temporal context on short time scales in a behavior-dependent manner and is positioned at the core of a brain-wide network updating sensorimotor representations in real time for flexible behavior, balancing specificity and regularization.
evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C76, C135-141 represent the main interpretive conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple analyses (feedback modulation, performance improvements, TTC-independent updating, regression effect tracking). The conclusions appropriately synthesize the empirical findings while acknowledging their interpretive nature.

result: The study proposes that the hippocampus encodes statistical regularities in a task-specific yet flexible format, balancing three objectives (specificity, regularization, flexibility), and that rapid encoding of temporal context manifests as the behavioral regression effect.
evaluation: Claims C1, C8, C15, and C16 represent the theoretical framework and hypotheses of the study. While these are speculative proposals (C1, C15, C16 marked as SPECULATION), they are well-motivated by prior literature and are subsequently supported by the empirical findings presented in the results.

result: The regression effect reflects a key behavioral adaptation for regularization that supports both current task performance and generalization to future scenarios, and this effect is hypothesized to be grounded in hippocampal activity.
evaluation: Claims C42, C128, and C129 combine interpretation of behavioral findings with hypothesis generation. The interpretation is well-supported by citations to prior work (Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2010; Roach et al., 2017) and is subsequently validated by the hippocampal activity analyses showing correlation with regression magnitude (C130).

result: The study builds on extensive prior literature showing that timing estimates rely on statistical regularities, that the hippocampus codes for time and temporal context, processes feedback, and has been implicated in domain-general learning and generalization.
evaluation: Claims C9-14, C71-75, C80-82, C93-94, C97-99, C111, C114-115, C124, C132-133 represent citations to prior work that establish the theoretical foundation. These are appropriately cited and accurately represent the prior literature, providing strong justification for the current study's hypotheses.

result: The study discusses potential mechanisms underlying the observed effects, including receptive field re-scaling, parallel updating of different task information types, and the relationship between temporal and spatial processing in the hippocampus.
evaluation: Claims C78-92, C95, C101-102, C108, C110, C112, C116-118, C121 represent mechanistic interpretations and speculations. While these are thoughtful and well-grounded in prior literature, they remain largely speculative (many marked as INFERENCE or SPECULATION). The proposed mechanisms (e.g., receptive field re-scaling, C113, C116, C117) are plausible but not directly tested in this study.

result: The study predicts that participants with stronger hippocampal updating activity should generalize better to new scenarios, such as when new intervals are tested.
evaluation: Claim C126 represents a prediction for future research that was not tested in the current study. While this is a logical prediction based on the findings, it remains speculative and would require additional experiments to validate.
